title: Sensory Skills and Communication
summary: Practise sequencing, imitation, tool choice, visual attention, comparison and pretend play.

subchapters.title: First, next, last
subchapters.body: Choose three familiar actions and say first, next and last while acting them out. Use objects, gestures or pictures to show each step. Keep the sequence short and repeat it consistently.
subchapters.takeaway: Predictable steps support understanding and communication.

questions.q: What helps a child understand a sequence?
questions.explanation: Short repeated steps are easier to anticipate.

quiz.q: How many steps should you start with?
quiz.explanation: Three steps give a clear beginning, middle and end.

quiz.q: What words can mark a sequence?
quiz.explanation: These words make order explicit.
Gestures and pictures can make meaning clearer.

quiz.q: Should the sequence change every time?
options: Only when the child is distressed
quiz.explanation: Repetition supports predictability.
Children can show understanding in different ways.

subchapters.title: Choose the tool
subchapters.body: Offer two tools for a simple task and let your child point, reach, gesture, use a picture or speak to choose. Give enough time to respond and use the selected tool together.
subchapters.takeaway: Communication does not need to be spoken.

options: Pointing, reaching, a picture or words

quiz.q: How many tools should you offer first?
quiz.explanation: Two tools create a manageable choice.

quiz.q: Should you wait for a response?
quiz.explanation: Processing time supports communication.
Reaching can communicate a preference.

quiz.q: What should you do with the selected tool?
quiz.explanation: Using the selected tool gives communication a meaningful result.
Communication should not be limited to speech.

chapters.title: Copy the movement
chapters.summary: Build imitation through one safe action at a time.

subchapters.title: Copy the movement
subchapters.body: Use one simple movement, wait and celebrate any attempt. Your child may copy immediately, later or in a different way. Never physically force imitation.
subchapters.takeaway: An attempt to copy is meaningful progress.

questions.q: What should an adult do after demonstrating?
questions.explanation: Waiting allows time to process and respond.

quiz.q: How many movements should you begin with?
quiz.explanation: One action keeps the task clear.
Forced movement can be unsafe and undermines trust.

quiz.q: Can a different movement be an attempt?
quiz.explanation: Attempts may not look exactly like the model.
Positive attention supports participation.
The activity supports imitation and shared attention.

chapters.title: Same or different
chapters.summary: Compare two objects using words or gestures.

subchapters.title: Same or different
subchapters.body: Place two objects together and ask whether they are the same or different. Accept pointing, matching, gestures or words. Start with very obvious differences.
subchapters.takeaway: Comparison can be shown in many ways.

questions.explanation: Clear contrasts are easier to understand.

quiz.q: How many objects should you compare first?
quiz.explanation: Two objects make the comparison clear.
Actions can show understanding.

quiz.q: Should the first difference be obvious?
quiz.explanation: Clear examples reduce confusion.
Pointing and gestures are valid communication.
The goal is to notice a shared or different feature.

chapters.title: Look and find
chapters.summary: Support visual scanning and target finding.

subchapters.title: Look and find
subchapters.body: Name a target and give your child time to scan. Reduce distractions, point only when needed and praise looking, checking and trying, not just a correct answer.

questions.q: What should you allow after naming a target?
questions.explanation: Scanning takes time, especially in a busy visual field.

quiz.explanation: Fewer distractions support visual attention.
Checking is a useful strategy.
Rushing can make visual search harder.
Attention and searching are the focus.
Small supports can help a child succeed.

chapters.title: Build and pretend
chapters.summary: Use open-ended building and pretend play.

subchapters.title: Build and pretend
subchapters.body: Build something simple with blocks or safe household items, then act out one pretend action together. Follow your child’s ideas. There is more than one right way to play.
subchapters.takeaway: Shared play can be flexible and child-led.

questions.explanation: Shared, flexible play respects the child's interests.

quiz.explanation: Simple safe materials are enough.

quiz.q: Is there one right way to play?
quiz.explanation: Play can be creative and individual.
Following interests supports engagement.
Use materials appropriate for the child and supervise as needed.
Pretend play can support flexible shared communication.
